Crime linkage: which crimes belong to one series

Source: R/lnkpr.R
lnkpr.Rd

Asks whether two crimes were committed by the same offender, from how far apart they are in space and time and how alike the offender behaved (the modus operandi: entry method, property taken, a weapon shown). For every pair of crimes it gives the distance, the time between them and the Jaccard similarity of their behaviours (the behaviours present in both over those present in either; 0 when neither shows any). On the pairs of solved crimes, linked when they belong to the same series, a logistic regression of being linked on the three measures is fitted and each measure's power to tell linked from unlinked pairs is the area under its ROC curve (AUC: the chance that a linked pair is closer, sooner or more alike than an unlinked one; 0.5 is no better than chance), as Bennell and Canter (2002) did for commercial burglaries. The fitted model then scores every pair, including those with an unsolved crime: prob is the estimated chance that the two are linked.

Usage

lnkpr(x, y = NULL, t, series, mo = NULL)

Arguments

x, y

The points in planar coordinates (project longitude and latitude with eqproj() first): x and y numeric vectors of equal length, or x a matrix or data frame with columns named x and y. At least two points; no missing values.

t

The time of each crime (days, say): finite numbers.

series

The series of each solved crime: labels, NA for an unsolved crime.

mo

NULL or the behaviours: a 0/1 or logical matrix, or a data frame or list of 0/1 columns, one row per crime.

Value

An object of class lnkpr, a list: coef, the logistic regression (term, est, se, z, p); auc, a named vector (dist, dt, jac, model); pairs, one row per pair of crimes (i, j, their rows, dist, dt, jac, linked, NA when either is unsolved, and prob); dev, the model's deviance; and nmo, the number of behaviours.

Details

The probabilities are those of the pairs in the data: series with many crimes give many linked pairs, and the share linked among pairs depends on how many series there are. The AUC of the model is in-sample and so optimistic.

References

Bennell, C. and Canter, D. V. (2002). Linking commercial burglaries by modus operandi: tests using regression and ROC analysis. Science & Justice, 42(3), 153-164. doi:10.1016/S1355-0306(02)71820-0

Examples

set.seed(9)
s <- rep(1:6, each = 5)
cx <- runif(6, 0, 5000)[s] + rnorm(30, 0, 1500)
cy <- runif(6, 0, 5000)[s] + rnorm(30, 0, 1500)
day <- runif(6, 0, 300)[s] + rnorm(30, 0, 60)
mo <- matrix(rbinom(30 * 5, 1, 0.3), 30)
sr <- ifelse(runif(30) < 0.2, NA, s)
r <- lnkpr(cbind(x = cx, y = cy), t = day, series = sr, mo = mo)
r$coef
#>          term           est           se          z            p
#> 1 (Intercept)  0.1466816977 0.4786319854  0.3064603 7.592542e-01
#> 2        dist -0.0001929138 0.0001228189 -1.5707178 1.162482e-01
#> 3          dt -0.0157565696 0.0033891231 -4.6491582 3.332925e-06
#> 4         jac  0.5344187921 0.8865379558  0.6028155 5.466315e-01
r$auc
#>      dist        dt       jac     model 
#> 0.5950469 0.7775642 0.5022617 0.7888726
